1.pericope_label: In the five and twentieth year of our captivity, in the beginning of the year, in the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after that the city was smitten, in the selfsame day the hand of the Lord was upon me, and brought me thither. In the visions of God brought he me into the land of Israel, and set me upon a very high mountain, by which was as the frame of a city on the south. And he brought me thither, and, behold, there was a man, whose appearance was like the appearance of brass, with a line of flax in his hand, and a measuring reed; and he stood in the gate. And the man said unto me, Son of man, behold with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears, and set thine heart upon all that I shall shew thee; for to the intent that I might shew them unto thee art thou brought hither: declare all that thou seest to the house of Israel.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat the last nine chapters as a single vision of the new temple, the new ordering of worship and the new division of the land, a section rounded off in itself and distinct in form from the preceding prophecies yet bound to them in substance, forming the half of the book in which the announcement of salvation is brought to completion; Ellicott observes that the prophet usually gives a year without naming its era and calls this one of our captivity, identifies the tenth of the first month as the day the paschal lamb was set apart and finds in it a fit season for a vision of the church to come, rejects the proposal that this was a jubilee year on the grounds that no evidence supports it, that the jubilee opened at the autumn fast, and that nothing shows years being counted from jubilees so early, denies that the phrase about the visions of God can describe anything with literal existence, refuses to identify the very high mountain with the temple hill since that hill is ringed by higher ground, corrects the preposition so that the structure stands upon the mountain, explains the southward bearing by the road a traveller from Chaldea would take, and distinguishes the flaxen line for long measures from the rod for short.

Gill reckons the date from the deportation by which the prophet dates everything and notes that he calls it our captivity because he shared it, and lingers on the address son of man as a reminder of the prophet's smallness that teaches the humility without which nothing is learned, while the familiarity of it removes the terror such an appearance would otherwise carry.

Clarke argues from the exiles' need for consolation that the minuteness of the description may have been meant to guide the builders of the second temple, no model of the first being thought to survive, adds the older Jewish rule that whatever was august in prophecy and unfulfilled near its own time was referred to the days of the Messiah, identifies the very high mountain with the hill where the old temple stood, describes the figure as polished brass throwing back the light with a glory about the head and leaves the choice open between an angel and Christ himself, and keeps the practical end in view, that all is to be told to the house of Israel so they may know how to build when the captivity is over; Wesley makes the tenth of the first month the day the paschal lamb was set aside, argues from the phrase about the visions of God that the transport was not corporeal, and identifies the measurer with the figure of the opening vision, whose name is the Branch.

Henry marks the interval, that fourteen years after the city fell the clearest prospect of deliverance arrives at the midnight of the captivity, says the prophet is set on the height as Moses was above the plains to look over a land promised a second time and not yet possessed, identifies what he sees as the frame of a city that turns out to be a temple as large as a city, sets it beside the last vision of Scripture, which shows a city with no temple in it, and concludes that the two come to much the same thing, a city for men to live in and a temple for God to live in; he also makes the measurer not a created angel but the one found in fashion as a man so that he might both show the gospel temple and build it.

debates.question: What season of the year does the date fix?

positions.position: The month of the passover, the tenth day being when the lamb was set apart — an apt season for a vision of the church to come; a jubilee year is to be rejected for want of evidence.
The first month, on the day the paschal lamb was taken up.
The point is the interval rather than the season: fourteen years after the city fell, at the midnight of the captivity.

debates.question: Who is the man whose appearance was like brass?

positions.position: Either an angel or a personal appearance of Christ; the choice is left open.
Not a created angel but Christ, found in fashion as a man so that he might both show the gospel temple and build it.
The figure of the opening vision, whose name is the Branch and whose office is to build.

outliers.claim: Denies that the mountain can be the temple hill, since that hill is ringed by higher ground, and takes the height instead as a mark of the site's spiritual importance in a description never meant to have literal existence.
Suggests a practical motive for the minuteness of the whole vision, that with no model of the first temple thought to survive, the description could guide the builders of the second.

5.pericope_label: And behold a wall on the outside of the house round about, and in the man’s hand a measuring reed of six cubits long by the cubit and an hand breadth: so he measured the breadth of the building, one reed; and the height, one reed. Then came he unto the gate which looketh toward the east, and went up the stairs thereof, and measured the threshold of the gate, which was one reed broad; and the other threshold of the gate, which was one reed broad. And every little chamber was one reed long, and one reed broad; and between the little chambers were five cubits; and the threshold of the gate by the porch of the gate within was one reed. He measured also the porch of the gate within, one reed. Then measured he the porch of the gate, eight cubits; and the posts thereof, two cubits; and the porch of the gate was inward. And the little chambers of the gate eastward were three on this side, and three on that side; they three were of one measure: and the posts had one measure on this side and on that side. And he measured the breadth of the entry of the gate, ten cubits; and the length of the gate, thirteen cubits. The space also before the little chambers was one cubit on this side, and the space was one cubit on that side: and the little chambers were six cubits on this side, and six cubits on that side. He measured then the gate from the roof of one little chamber to the roof of another: the breadth was five and twenty cubits, door against door. He made also posts of threescore cubits, even unto the post of the court round about the gate. And from the face of the gate of the entrance unto the face of the porch of the inner gate were fifty cubits. And there were narrow windows to the little chambers, and to their posts within the gate round about, and likewise to the arches: and windows were round about inward: and upon each post were palm trees.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep to the plan of the east gate, giving the guard-rooms a rod square apiece with five cubits between them and three to each side; Ellicott insists that each of the six cubits of the rod carried its own handbreadth rather than the handbreadth being added once to the whole, explains the addition by the fact that the cubit in ordinary use after the return differed from the older standard, as a chronicler implies by dating measurements to the first measure, declines to fix the length exactly since estimates run from eighteen inches to twenty-four and settles on twenty for convenience, giving a rod of about ten feet, and says the equal thickness and height of the surrounding wall are there for the symmetry of the measures, noting that its length is withheld until near the end of the chapter.

Gill observes that the wall is the first thing shown after the architect himself and reads it by the purpose stated later in the chapter, to divide the sanctuary from the profane place, which he glosses as the church from the world; on the little chambers he refuses both the obvious spiritual readings, the heart of the believer and the mansions of heaven, and makes them the particular congregations planted in every quarter, called chambers for their secrecy since the hidden ones are there; he reports and rejects the older opinion that the sixty-cubit posts stood between the outer wall and the building for ornament, preferring the columns carrying the arch of the gate; and he explains the narrow windows both mechanically, the walls being splayed so the light should spread further, and allegorically, as the word and ordinances by which light gets into the churches.

Clarke computes the rod at ten feet six inches from a cubit of twenty and a half inches plus a palm, infers from the wall's being as broad as it is high that it was a parapet carried all round, and observes that a building on rising ground needs steps outside each door, the chapter having them between court and court as well; Wesley keeps the common cubit of eighteen inches, makes the wall the outermost one about the whole hill, points out that the threshold could not be measured until the surveyor had climbed and that the number of steps comes out at ten, eight or seven according to where he is supposed to stand, takes the guard-rooms for lodgings of the priests and Levites during their courses with rails set a cubit in front for benches, works out that each chamber had a door east and west set so exactly that with all open one could see through to the house, takes the sixty cubits for height and supposes two storeys above the arch, and says the windows narrowed inward with more set under the arches.

Henry makes the reed six cubits of the sanctuary, that cubit being a handbreadth longer than the common one at twenty-two inches against eighteen, and reports but rejects the rival view that the reed was six common cubits with one handbreadth added to the whole; he gives the wall three yards each way and draws from it both separation and protection, adding that if such a thickness will not secure the place God will be a wall of fire round it; he explains that the east gate comes first because entry was at the lower end, the holiest place standing at the west against the heathen habit of worshipping toward the sunrise; and he notices that the outer court of the Gentiles is left unmeasured, on a suggestion he reports, because the confluence of Gentiles in gospel times would leave its worshippers past numbering.

debates.question: How long was the measuring reed?

positions.position: Six sacred cubits of twenty-two inches each, the handbreadth belonging to every cubit rather than to the reed as a whole.
Six cubits each carrying its own handbreadth, but the cubit itself is unfixable; twenty inches is a convenient figure, making the rod about ten feet.
About ten feet six inches, from a cubit of twenty and a half inches with a palm added.
Six common cubits of eighteen inches, with a handbreadth added.

debates.question: What are the little chambers along the gateway?

positions.position: The particular congregations planted in every quarter of the world, called chambers for their secrecy; expressly not the believer's heart nor the mansions of heaven.
Lodgings for the priests and Levites during their courses, with rails in front for benches.
Guard-rooms of the gate, a rod square apiece with five cubits between and three to each side.

outliers.claim: Notices that the court of the Gentiles is never measured at all, and reports the suggestion that it was left out because the confluence of Gentiles in gospel times would leave its worshippers past numbering.
Derives the number of steps from where the surveyor is imagined to stand, giving ten, eight or seven, since the threshold at the top could not be measured until he had climbed.

17.pericope_label: Then brought he me into the outward court, and, lo, there were chambers, and a pavement made for the court round about: thirty chambers were upon the pavement. And the pavement by the side of the gates over against the length of the gates was the lower pavement. Then he measured the breadth from the forefront of the lower gate unto the forefront of the inner court without, an hundred cubits eastward and northward. And the gate of the outward court that looked toward the north, he measured the length thereof, and the breadth thereof. And the little chambers thereof were three on this side and three on that side; and the posts thereof and the arches thereof were after the measure of the first gate: the length thereof was fifty cubits, and the breadth five and twenty cubits. And their windows, and their arches, and their palm trees, were after the measure of the gate that looketh toward the east; and they went up unto it by seven steps; and the arches thereof were before them. And the gate of the inner court was over against the gate toward the north, and toward the east; and he measured from gate to gate an hundred cubits. After that he brought me toward the south, and behold a gate toward the south: and he measured the posts thereof and the arches thereof according to these measures. And there were windows in it and in the arches thereof round about, like those windows: the length was fifty cubits, and the breadth five and twenty cubits. And there were seven steps to go up to it, and the arches thereof were before them: and it had palm trees, one on this side, and another on that side, upon the posts thereof. And there was a gate in the inner court toward the south: and he measured from gate to gate toward the south an hundred cubits. And he brought me to the inner court by the south gate: and he measured the south gate according to these measures; And the little chambers thereof, and the posts thereof, and the arches thereof, according to these measures: and there were windows in it and in the arches thereof round about: it was fifty cubits long, and five and twenty cubits broad. And the arches round about were five and twenty cubits long, and five cubits broad. And the arches thereof were toward the utter court; and palm trees were upon the posts thereof: and the going up to it had eight steps. And he brought me into the inner court toward the east: and he measured the gate according to these measures. And the little chambers thereof, and the posts thereof, and the arches thereof, were according to these measures: and there were windows therein and in the arches thereof round about: it was fifty cubits long, and five and twenty cubits broad. And the arches thereof were toward the outward court; and palm trees were upon the posts thereof, on this side, and on that side: and the going up to it had eight steps. And he brought me to the north gate, and measured it according to these measures;

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe cells and a mosaic floor laid on both sides of the gate-buildings, of a width matching their length and running along the inside of the court wall, so that the paving did not cover the whole area, and remark that the northern and southern gate-buildings are described very briefly, only the principal parts being given with a note that they matched the east; Ellicott points out that the plan assigns neither court to any class of worshipper though the inner may be assumed for the priests and the outer for the people, that neither size nor position is given for the thirty chambers so that their arrangement must be inferred from the symmetry, that such rooms for officiating priests and for storing tithes are mentioned in connection with both earlier houses, that the lower pavement is so called against an inner pavement on a higher level and its width equals the projection of the gateways, and that the hundred cubits are measured from a clearly stated starting point to an unstated finishing point, a doubt resolved by the later verses which say from gate to gate. He also notes that the gates of the inner court are the outer ones reversed, with the porches facing each other, that they have one step more so that the two flights make the fifteen which in the later house led from court to court, and that the verse giving the arches as twenty-five cubits by five is probably spurious, since the term should mean wall projections, the dimensions fit nothing, the statement is unparalleled among the gate descriptions and the Greek omits it.

Gill matches the outer court to the old court where good and bad worshipped together and takes it for the visible church with its wheat and tares, gives both explanations of the lower pavement without choosing between them, that it lay below the inner court's paving or that its middle rose in a slight convex so the dirt was carried to the sides, makes the two levels the believer's walk by faith and his walk in the ordinances, and turns the repetition of the gate measurements into doctrine, that the churches of the latter day will all be built on one pattern with their light and flourishing condition alike everywhere.

Clarke says the same measures were used throughout and corrects one term, since what is called an arch should be a porch, the arch being unknown at that date; Wesley calls this the second court about the house, distributes the thirty chambers fifteen to each side of the gate and makes them store-houses as well as lodgings, prefers the convex explanation of the lower pavement and adds that the lower side paving served for state as well as cleanliness, reads the hundred cubits as the ground between the inner front of one gate and the outer front of the next, concludes the court was square, and notes that a diversity of courts may put us in mind of the diversity of gifts in the church and of degrees of glory in heaven. Clarke also treats that same disputed verse as damaged rather than spurious, holding that the breadth ought to read twenty-five as the parallel verses show and that the word for twenty has dropped out, and adding that the whole verse is missing from several manuscripts, one of them his own, where a later hand supplied it in the margin.

Henry presses the uniformity of the gates, that the inner matched the outer down to the engraving on the posts, and draws from it that the work of grace is the same in substance in the grown Christian as in the beginner; he also observes what is missing, that neither court has a gate on the west, though the mention of western porters suggests the first house had them and a historian says the second had none.

debates.question: How were the thirty chambers of the outer court arranged?

positions.position: Neither size nor position is given; from the general symmetry, ten on each of the three sides free of the temple buildings.
Fifteen on each side of the gate, serving as store-houses as well as lodgings.
Cells set on both sides of the gate-buildings along the inside of the court wall, with the paving matching their length.

debates.question: What should be done with the verse giving the arches as twenty-five cubits by five?

positions.position: Emend it: the breadth should read twenty-five, the word for twenty having dropped out, and the verse is missing from several manuscripts entirely.
Suspect the whole verse: the term should mean wall projections, the dimensions fit nothing, the statement is unparalleled among the gates, and the Greek omits it.
Take the figure as the height of the frontispiece facing the outer court, a portico over the eight steps.

outliers.claim: Corrects the received rendering on historical grounds, since the term translated arch must mean a porch, the arch being unknown at the date of the vision.
Notes that neither court has a western gate, though western porters imply the first house had one and a historian reports a solid wall there in the second.

38.pericope_label: And the chambers and the entries thereof were by the posts of the gates, where they washed the burnt offering. And in the porch of the gate were two tables on this side, and two tables on that side, to slay thereon the burnt offering and the sin offering and the trespass offering. And at the side without, as one goeth up to the entry of the north gate, were two tables; and on the other side, which was at the porch of the gate, were two tables. Four tables were on this side, and four tables on that side, by the side of the gate; eight tables, whereupon they slew their sacrifices. And the four tables were of hewn stone for the burnt offering, of a cubit and an half long, and a cubit and an half broad, and one cubit high: whereupon also they laid the instruments wherewith they slew the burnt offering and the sacrifice. And within were hooks, an hand broad, fastened round about: and upon the tables was the flesh of the offering. And without the inner gate were the chambers of the singers in the inner court, which was at the side of the north gate; and their prospect was toward the south: one at the side of the east gate having the prospect toward the north. And he said unto me, This chamber, whose prospect is toward the south, is for the priests, the keepers of the charge of the house. And the chamber whose prospect is toward the north is for the priests, the keepers of the charge of the altar: these are the sons of Zadok among the sons of Levi, which come near to the Lord to minister unto him. So he measured the court, an hundred cubits long, and an hundred cubits broad, foursquare; and the altar that was before the house. And he brought me to the porch of the house, and measured each post of the porch, five cubits on this side, and five cubits on that side: and the breadth of the gate was three cubits on this side, and three cubits on that side. The length of the porch was twenty cubits, and the breadth eleven cubits; and he brought me by the steps whereby they went up to it: and there were pillars by the posts, one on this side, and another on that side.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch follow the text of the sacrificial arrangements, a cell with its door where the burnt offering was washed, two tables on each side within the porch, two more at each shoulder outside, eight in all, and four of hewn stone by the steps to carry the instruments, and record the porch of the house at twenty cubits by eleven with a pillar at either post and steps leading up to it; Ellicott explains why the slaying is done at the north gate but inside the outer court, since the law had each offerer kill his own victim at the north of the altar while here the Levites do it, so the work is placed where the offerer and the people can watch, separates the eight tables of one verse from the four and four of another to reach twelve in all, prefers by the porch to in the porch since the porch is too small for two tables a side and a thoroughfare is no place for slaughter, and accepts the traditional rendering of a word found only once elsewhere, where it is translated pots, as hooks for hanging the flesh once prepared, on the ground that whatever is meant stands within the porch and so cannot belong to the tables outside.

Gill sets the first four tables in the gaps between the little chambers, two to a side, and treats the later verses as the same tables named again so that their position and use may be observed more carefully; he takes the hooks for fittings on the gate posts near the washing room and describes the later slaughter house to show what is meant, stone pillars carrying cedar boards with three rows of iron hooks a handbreadth out, a lamb on the lowest row, a ram on the middle and a bullock on the highest; he makes the singers' chambers a place for those who sing with the spirit and the understanding, fitting them as inward-court worshippers; he reads the porch as a covering from wind, storm and heat, and so an emblem of the hiding place from tempest and from a fiery law, adding that it was thought a place where the priests prayed before going in; and he ends with the editorial judgement that these last two verses belong with what follows and a new chapter ought properly to have begun there.

Clarke names the court measured here the priests' court, observes that the gate of the porch was evidently a folding door, and gives a historian's dimensions for the vestibule at twenty cubits by ten; Wesley has the hooks fastened to walls near the tables for hanging the carcass while it was further prepared, and identifies the keepers of the charge as those responsible for the house during their courses, with others appointed to keep the fire alight on the altar.

Henry takes the tables for the point of the whole passage, observing that no altar is described until a much later chapter and thinking the delay deliberate, since the one altar of the law was to give way to a multitude of tables and no altar appears in this house until the glory has taken possession, Christ being himself the altar that sanctifies the gift; he adds that nothing of the kind is recorded in the tabernacle or the first temple, so that the provision of them here intimates how many spiritual sacrifices would be brought and how many hands employed in offering them.

debates.question: How many sacrificial tables were there, and where did they stand?

positions.position: Eight, two on each side within the porch and two at each shoulder outside, with four more of hewn stone by the steps for the instruments.
Twelve, the eight of one verse being distinct from those of another; and beside the porch rather than in it, since a thoroughfare is no place for slaughter.
Four set in the gaps between the little chambers, two to a side, the later verses naming the same tables again.

debates.question: What were the dimensions of the porch of the house?

positions.position: Twenty cubits by eleven, with a pillar at either post and steps up to it.
Twenty cubits by ten, on a historian's authority, the gate being a folding door.

outliers.claim: Reads the absence of any altar until much later in the vision as deliberate, the single altar of the law giving way to a multitude of tables and no altar appearing until the glory has taken possession.
Makes a textual-division judgement, that the closing two verses belong with the following chapter and the break has been put in the wrong place.
